newsitem.title: USA: US rates steady, analysts see Fed tightening bias.
newsitem.headline: US rates steady, analysts see Fed tightening bias.

text.p: The Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady Wednesday, but analysts said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) might have adopted, or maybe kept, a bias towards tightening during its July meeting.
"It's very rare for the Fed to raise rates just once," said William Ford, a former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

The risks for the economy are still seen tilted to the upside, even though the Fed opted to maintain a steady policy in response to a substantial economic slowdown in the second quarter and a benign inflation environment, experts said.
The Fed hiked the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25 for the first time in more than two years. It stood pat in the May and in the July FOMC meetings.

Despite recent signs of deceleration, analysts said the economy might rebound in the second half as businesses continue to invest, manufacturers build up inventories, and consumers resume a buying spree after a three-month hiatus.

If true, analysts said the Fed is likely to respond to higher demand by tightening monetary policy in an effort to ward off possible inflationary pressures. The FOMC will meet next on August 19, then on September 30.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth is widely forecast to have slowed to somewhere close to 2.0 percent in the second quarter after a red-hot 5.9 percent expansion rate in the first three months of the year.
Analysts said any rebound to economic growth levels above 3.0 percent on a quarterly basis was likely to trigger a tightening move by the central bank.

"You would have to see the economy somewhere above 3.0 percent for the Fed to tighten again. I'm not sure how far above, but it will have to be faster than three," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
But for now, everyone acknowledges inflation is still a missing person.

Although varying in degree, all economists interviewed for this article agreed the economy might have a bit more inflationary resistance now that U.S. markets are more open and competition more globalized.

"It's absolutely wonderful for our economy that we've got this increased global competition," said Ford, who now chairs the finance department at the Middle Tennessee University and is a senior economic advisor for TeleCheck Inc.
Analysts also said that despite the unusually tight labor markets -- latest data put the unemployment rate at 4.8 percent in May -- inflationary wage pressures have been extremely scattered.

"We want the tightest labor market we can get without running any risk of inflation, and maybe we've got that now," said Robert Solow, professor emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

"Maybe it could get a tiny notch tigher and still not generate any inflation. So my hope is that the Fed will continue to wait and see ... My picture is that right now is that it ain't broken, so it shouldn't be fixed," Solow added.
